title: The Lifecycle of LLM-as-a-Judge: Building, Aligning, and Monitoring at scale
abstract: By Emma Yanyang Kong , JJ Tan , Ishan Gupta , Lars Olds , Claire Campbell , David Fagnan , Ratna Kavuri , Rohan Gosain , Veli Balin , Minsu Jang , Louis Garcia Introduction Any team generating text with an LLM at scale hits the same problem. You cannot evaluate everything manually. You don't know which outputs are great, which are mediocre, and which are harmful, because you simply cannot read them all. The standard solution is LLM-as-a-Judge , a second model that scores the first model’s output as a proxy for human raters. It is fast, cheap, and easy to deploy. However, it introduces a new and critical question: Who evaluates the evaluator? Furthermore, if the judge drifts, quietly degrading and starting to approve bad output, nothing downstream will flag it. This post is about how we solve that problem, by building, aligning, and continuously monitoring LLM judges so they stay trustworthy over time. Our core principle is simple: An LLM judge must never operate alone. It has to be anchored in human judgment. We keep a human-in-the-loop (HITL) at every phase of the lifecycle. Humans define what “good” means, create the labeled benchmark datasets to train and validate the judge, monitor its behavior while it runs in the system, and review and approve any updates before they’re rolled out. We believe: A reliable LLM judge is not a static artifact. It has a lifecycle. It needs to be built against trusted human labels, aligned with human preference and reasoning, run under human-set policy, and maintained as the data and usage pattern shift. Each of these stages has human owners. In the sections below, we walk through these four phases, the key design decisions in each, and the lessons we’d share with a team building their own LLM judge, using one concrete task as our running example: recommendation explanations. A recommendation explanation is a short natural-language message that accompanies a recommended item, and it shapes how users perceive and trust a recommender system. In our work, an explanation is human-readable evidence for why a title was recommended based on what the member has previously watched, shown on the title’s detail page, which is the screen a member reaches by selecting a title from the homepage. We focus on similarity-based explanations, which connect a recommended title to one reference title the member has interacted with via shared attributes such as genre and tone. For example, A funny, heartfelt holiday romance about love and new beginnings, much like “My Secret Santa.” Quality matters here because a misleading or poorly grounded explanation erodes the very trust the explanation is meant to build. Everything that follows comes out of a series of controlled, user-facing online experiments we ran on the explanation feature, including a month-long experiment on the Netflix mobile app. In these tests we used an LLM to generate explanations, hundreds of thousands a week across a constantly changing catalog. Manually reviewing them at this scale isn’t feasible, so we deployed a second LLM to evaluate them. What counts as a good explanation is specific to our task. However, the way we build, align, and monitor the LLM judge for evaluating explanations should be reusable and generalizable across different tasks. The Lifecycle at a Glance Figure 1 summarizes the four phases of our LLM-judge lifecycle and the data flow connecting them. Figure 1. The four-phase lifecycle of an LLM judge, and the data that flows between the phases. We start with Birth: Benchmark Data Creation , where human experts craft hard or near-boundary examples and human raters label them with pass/fail decisions and written rationales. We augment this with LLM-generated gray-area examples to build a richer benchmark dataset. Next, in the second phase of Training: LLM Judge Development , we tune the LLM judge to align with human labels and rationales from the Birth phase, using self-reflection to identify mismatches between the judge and hum

title: Netflix Stratum Media Processing: Automated Container Right-Sizing
abstract: By Violetta Pidvolotska and Naveen Mareddy Stratum is Netflix’s internal serverless media processing platform, shaped by over a decade of experience developing large-scale distributed systems. It powers a wide range of media workloads — including encoding, packaging, inspection, and quality scoring — behind playback, advertising, studio workflows, AI embeddings, and more. Engineers develop Stratum functions by packaging application code and OS dependencies into OCI images. Stratum then schedules these containers as batch jobs on Netflix’s Titus compute platform, with upstream services triggering function executions. Every day, Stratum manages hundreds of thousands of containers across bursty, high-throughput, and latency-sensitive workloads. As Netflix’s core media processing platform, this load needs to scale as new content formats enter the catalog, such as podcasts , live events , sports , ads , or regional ingests like TF1 in France . To request resources for these functions, owners specify their CPU, memory, disk, and network limits as YAML configuration, as shown below: functionName: VideoEncoder.encodeV1 resources: numCpus: 8 memoryInMB: 18000 diskSizeInMB: 50000 networkInMbps: 1000 Maintaining optimal values manually is challenging amidst evolving Netflix infrastructure, EC2 instance upgrades, and application-level changes. Consequently, configs are often over-provisioned upfront or slowly drift away from their ideal values over time. Mis-sized configurations are a universal pain of large-scale serverless platforms, causing additional cognitive load for function builders and operational costs for platform owners. In this post, we share how we built the Stratum Resource Tuner (SRT) — an automated system that safely right-sizes running containers in production without human intervention. We will walk through real-world examples, our safety architecture, and what we learned when an automated change went wrong. The Challenge: Over-Provisioning When engineers write a new Stratum function, they typically copy a resource YAML from an existing function or size it for the absolute worst-case scenario. Once running in production, engineers rarely revisit these configurations until a failure occurs, prompting them to over-provision resources out of an abundance of caution. Manual resource tuning does not scale for the following reasons: High Operational Friction: Downsizing requires days of manual metric monitoring and trial-and-error testing, diverting valuable engineering cycles away from other high-impact work. If a cut goes too far, engineers face production incidents — making manual tuning a high-risk, low-reward task. Continuous Infrastructure & Codec Evolution: Cloud providers regularly upgrade their hardware. A resource allocation that was optimal on an older hardware generation quietly becomes inefficient on newer hardware. At the same time, Netflix continuously advances media standards and improves encoding algorithms (such as AV1 , AV2, and spatial audio ). An allocation tuned for one codec might not be optimal when an improved algorithm is released. Dynamic Workload Evolution: As Netflix expands into new media types — such as streaming video podcasts , sports, interactive AI-adapted ad formats , and major broadcaster integrations like TF1 in France — media processing footprints can change unpredictably, rendering static container resource limits imprecise. Rising Industry Hardware Costs: Driven by massive global AI infrastructure demand, server hardware and DRAM prices continue to climb, making idle container memory significantly more expensive to waste. Compounding Platform Scale: At Netflix scale, even minor over-provisioning multiplies exponentially across hundreds of thousands of daily container executions, compounding wasted capacity across the entire Stratum platform. This Week in AI: Expanding the Possibilities
abstract: New AI tools are making business data easier to explore. They’re also giving researchers new ways to study disease outbreaks and physical systems. On the latest episode of This Week in AI , we examined developments from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mistral, new research on the economics of robotics, and how scientists are using AI to tackle difficult problems. New AI tools put more capabilities directly in users’ hands OpenAI’s new Intelligent UI feature lets ChatGPT generate visual explanations and interactive tools directly in conversations. With the launch of MCP Events , supported connected applications can notify ChatGPT when something happens. If a user has asked ChatGPT to watch for that event, it can follow their instructions and take requested actions without waiting for another prompt. Anthropic’s Claude Dashboards brings natural-language queries and interactive visualizations to company data. Claude Motion adds another visual capability, turning reports and charts into editable animations. Self-service dashboards can create a range of problems though. For example, employees may reference incomplete data or apply different definitions to the same metric, then share their results as authoritative. As more employees take on exploratory analysis, BI teams will need to expand their role by maintaining reliable data and shared definitions, setting clear governance and access rules, helping employees interpret results responsibly, and monitoring how dashboards are used. Beyond the big two, Mistral previewed Large 4 , a trillion-parameter open-weight model designed for coding, agents, and multimodal tasks. The company plans to release the model’s weights soon, giving developers access to another large model for building and running AI applications. As AI agents gain access to more applications and company data, organizations will need clearer rules about what those agents can access and when humans should intervene. Recent internal tests at Anthropic showed how difficult it can be to control agents once they have access to external systems. The company reported cases of Claude circumventing restrictions, including copying server files and submitting fabricated forms, and subsequently restricted live internet access in internal tests until they’re better able to monitor their systems. OpenAI also announced plans for text watermarking in the EU , though editing and short passages can make watermarks difficult to detect reliably. Robotics research puts automation forecasts in perspective A new Anthropic study offered a useful counterpoint to predictions of widespread job displacement. Researchers found that existing robots could perform tasks accounting for roughly 34% of US work hours, but doing so would be cost competitive for just 0.3% of work hours. Most of these tasks take place in structured environments such as factories, where robots can operate more reliably than in unpredictable settings. When researchers combined the potential exposure of cognitive work to language models with physical work exposed to robotics, the share of work hours potentially affected reached 81%. For employers and policymakers, exposure figures help identify which tasks could change, but they don’t predict how many jobs automation will eliminate. Deployment costs, working conditions, and the need for human judgment will influence how quickly employers adopt these technologies . As we discussed during the audience Q&A, jobs are already changing, particularly in technical fields, even without evidence of massive displacement. For now, employers may get more value from helping workers develop new skills than from planning around speculative job-loss forecasts. AI is opening new avenues for scientific research AI is helping researchers tackle problems in mathematics, biology, space, and public health. title: Code Review After Code Gets Cheap
abstract: In my previous article , I argued that agentic development needs enough specification to make correctness checkable. A quick prompt can get implementation started quickly, but someone still has to decide whether the result does what we wanted. I left a fairly practical question unanswered, though. Once the agent has written the code, how should we review it? You can give an agent a clear task and get back a serious implementation with tests. The build passes and the code looks reasonable. Now somebody has to approve the pull request, and that person has roughly the same amount of time they had before code generation became cheap. Reading every changed line is one way to approach this. But if each increase in generated code requires a similar increase in human inspection, review will keep limiting how many changes we can accept. We need a way to decide where that inspection is worth the effort. My approach is to make evidence a condition of accepting agent-generated code. Agree on the intended behavior and the expected blast radius before implementation starts. Then use the evidence to check for drift and decide which parts of the code need direct inspection. So far, that may sound like test-driven development. But what happens when every test passes and the agent has added behavior nobody asked for? A small diff can have a large blast radius Let’s use a small fictional example. Suppose we are adding an approval step to a refund service. Refunds above €100 require approval from an authorized employee before the service sends the payment request. Exactly €100 does not require this additional approval. The existing rules about who can request a refund continue to apply. An agent implements the approval step and adds tests. While updating the payment integration, it also adds retries after a timeout. That seems reasonable enough. Network calls fail, and retrying them is a familiar engineering practice. But a timeout leaves us with another question. The provider may have issued the refund before its response was lost. Sending the request again could issue a second refund. Whether that can happen depends on how the provider handles repeated requests and how our code uses that behavior. The approval feature may be correct while the added retry introduces a separate problem. I can see a human review focusing only on the requested feature and easily missing the new decision about payment behavior. By blast radius, I mean how far the effects of a mistake can spread. If the agent puts the retry in a shared payment client, it may affect every refund, including those below the approval threshold. The change now reaches beyond the feature we asked for. Counting the changed lines won’t tell us that. Treat blast radius as a review criterion on its own. Establish which operations a change is allowed to affect, then check whether the implementation stays within that boundary. Also consider how hard a mistake would be to undo. Deploying the previous version won’t recover money that has already been refunded twice. Look for drift in both directions This is the kind of drift I want a review process to expose. We need to check that the requested behavior exists and examine additional behavior that could affect the system. There is an established name for following these relationships in both directions: bidirectional traceability. NASA’s software engineering guidance describes tracing requirements through implementation and verification, including finding functionality that has no parent requirement. I think that the basic idea translates quite well to an ordinary pull request. For each important requirement, we should be able to find the implementation and the checks that support it. Looking back from the implementation, we should be able to explain why a change to behavior belongs in this pull request. An extra private method will usually need little discussion. A retry that changes how money moves needs a reason we can review. Of course, an unpl

title: Generative AI in the Real World: Observability for AI with Charity Majors
abstract: AI makes it possible to generate code faster than teams can understand and support it. In this episode, Honeycomb cofounder and CTO Charity Majors joined Ben to discuss how that shift changes the work of building reliable software. Charity explained how observability helps teams connect changes with outcomes, why nondeterministic systems need “more rigor, not less,” and how traces can show the decisions agents make along the way. Over their wide-ranging conversation, she and Ben also covered automatic instrumentation with OpenTelemetry, why we should think of ourselves as “owners on the loop,” the limits of AI in debugging and SRE, and broader industry concerns like the pressure AI hype places on engineering teams and why maintenance, not speed, builds “enduring value.” About the Generative AI in the Real World podcast: In 2023, ChatGPT put AI on everyone’s agenda. In 2026, the challenge will be turning those agendas into reality. In Generative AI in the Real World , Ben Lorica interviews leaders who are building with AI. Learn from their experience to help put AI to work in your enterprise. Check out other episodes of this podcast on the O’Reilly learning platform or follow us on YouTube , Spotify , Apple , or wherever you get your podcasts. Takeaways 00.59 . “Observability is for unknown unknowns.” Monitoring is a way to set thresholds and alert on expected conditions. Observability supports open-ended investigation to answer questions you didn’t know to ask and “find things you didn’t expect.” When AI code generation became capable enough to change software work, observability best practices had to evolve, which is one reason why the second edition of Observability Engineering , which Charity coauthored with Liz Fong-Jones and George Miranda, more than doubled in size. 05.24 . Cheap code shifts the work to understanding and support. AI can quickly produce implementation, tests, and documentation, but teams still need to understand what they built and agreed to support, and how their users are experiencing the product. As generating lines of code becomes “effectively free and instant,” validation, review, and operational support can constrain a team’s pace. Of course, Charity wryly noted, so can “every other part of the software development lifecycle.” 06.24 . The people who take the credit for AI-assisted work should be able to explain it. AI-generated results (and the papers describing them) complicate authorship, expertise, and the academic training process, something that’s become a particular point of consternation for mathematicians of late. If someone is claiming a result they accomplished with the help of AI, they should be able to present it to peers, Charity and Ben agreed. When AI handles entry-level problems, professions may need new ways for junior practitioners to develop mastery, but Charity is skeptical we’ll run out of problems to solve: In the same way that I’ve made peace with the idea that cars are faster than I can walk or run, I have made peace with the fact that computers can compute better than I can. . . .That doesn’t mean that there’s no value in the practice, or the discipline, or the learning, or the rigor. It just means that this is one of the things that humans are no longer the best at. But there are a lot of things that we are the best at, and being the best at something isn’t all of what makes it worth doing. 15.56 Nondeterministic systems require “more rigor, not less.” As Charity noted, “The future of software is both determinism and nondeterminism. It really is about using these superpowers that we’ve been given to build those feedback loops. And observability is really the feedback loop of feedback loops.” It’s what connects actions with outcomes and helps teams learn what happened after they make a change. Her analogy: It’s like we’ve all been riding lawnmowers and just kind of putt-putt, putt-putt, putt-putt along down the road. And now, all of a sudden, our lawnmower has a Ferrari moto

title: Agentic Code Quality
abstract: The following article originally appeared on Addy Osmani’s Elevate blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission. For much of human history, we’ve evaluated code quality via code review: Someone reads what you wrote and makes sure it’s clean, thoughtful, fast, understandable, and tests well. For agents, that approach doesn’t scale well; there’s just too much code for anyone to read. As a result, more and more of our quality checks have to happen in the harness, environment, and operating system around the agent. I still read and review code, but am very intentional about where I am comfortable with constraints as the check. Software quality now depends on the constraints you set around your agents. Speaking of quality, agents are writing your code. Sonar gives you the quality gates to make it shippable. I had a coding agent build a slick app, then asked an agent to review it—twice. The reviews disagreed, and a re-run gave a third answer. You can’t gate a merge on a coin flip. Sonar runs the same complete check on every commit: deep cross-file analysis, a map of where the risk lives, and a quality gate that holds every human and agent to one bar. Try Sonar. Sponsored by Sonar. Constraints define what the system is allowed to do by throwing tests and deterministic constraints at an agent’s proposals. It’s by setting and maintaining these constraints that we build loops that reliably deliver high-quality production software, even when agents are creating hundreds of thousands or millions of changes every single day. We call these constraints quality gates, and they take many forms. They include conventional unit tests, property tests, and acceptance tests. They include mutation testing, where we generate variations of code, run it against the same tests, and make sure that people aren’t sneaking bugs in that we’re missing. They’re metrics around code quality, such as cyclomatic complexity and line length, that help keep things readable. Constraints also play an important role in what proposals the system will accept and apply as code changes. By the time a change proposal moves from the interpreter running the agent to the agent controller and out to production, we’ve done enough checks on it to be confident that it’s safe to ship and the impact of its change is well within the scope of the agent. Guillermo’s list is a good test for whether you can afford to skip reading. Notice that every “yes” is really a statement about how low the stakes are: no users, throwaway code, prototype. Once the stakes go up, something has to read the code. If it isn’t you on every diff then it has to be the constraints. An agent can propose anything. Your constraints decide whether a proposal is safe enough, correct, scoped, and useful, for you and your team to ship. This model offers a lot but also leaves out many pieces, and those omissions are worth thinking about today. One issue is autonomy ; agents might apply their intentions well but may fail when there’s missing information or when what they try to do is ambiguous. That applies both to the task itself and to how it’s parameterized by the harness, environment, and other components. Many of the reasons that humans fail to ship great code are shared with what agents might do: brittle environments that don’t hold up under script-driven stress, nondeterministic builds, missing permissions, and weak tests. This motivates a better environment that gives agents trustworthy feedback, allows for low-damage failure modes, and makes it easier to progressively build up success. The environment we’re after is one where an agent can do real work, get feedback it can trust, and fail without doing much damage. The other important issue is trust. title: Why Does AI Write Like Yoda?
abstract: I use AI for writing all the time. But not because it’s good at writing. In fact, just the opposite is true. AI is so reliably bad at writing that I’ve actually taken advantage of that, and made its bad writing an integral part of my writing process. I’ve written a lot of books and articles over the years, and while I used to start with an outline, I don’t anymore. These days I do a lot of brain dumping and brainstorming and talking out loud to an AI, working out what I think about something. I accumulate a lot of notes and ideas, and run a lot of experiments, and at some point, if I’m lucky, I decide there might be an article somewhere in all of that. Then I ask the AI to take everything I’ve given it and write a draft. And that AI-generated draft is universally terrible. Like, some of the worst writing you can imagine. Which is exactly what I want. Instead of an outline, I get an entire “article” or “chapter” (or, at least, a weird facsimile of one), with paragraphs that express complete thoughts that I gave the AI. Granted, those paragraphs are full of obvious AI tics, like how it uses em dashes to squish two unrelated sentences together, or weird staccato sentences one after another, or these insufferable parades of sentence fragments. Maybe the worst tic is that half of the paragraphs AI generates have an extra sentence that doesn’t actually say anything, but just delivers a forced conclusion with fake “punchiness.” I guess maybe AIs were trained on a lot of bad writing? Well, whatever, it works for me. The reason I love that type of obviously bad AI writing is because when I’m looking at one of its paragraphs, it’s immediately obvious that an AI wrote it. I’ve been thinking of it as a kind of an improved “ lorem ipsum ” that lets me see how my article will look, while still serving as a functional placeholder. That lets me use it the way I would use an outline: I can move parts of the article around, make sure it flows correctly, and then replace ALL of the bad AI writing with (hopefully) decent human writing, just like I used to do with bullets in my old outlines. One weird side-effect of writing this way is that it’s made me very sensitive to the different kinds of AI tics and tells. And I think the weirdest and most frustrating one is “Yoda-speak,” where the AI literally talks like Yoda. It’s weird, kind of hilarious, annoying, and pervasive, but most of all, it’s fascinating. Why does the AI keep talking like Yoda? What causes it? Can we do anything about it? (Do we even want to? It certainly makes it easy to identify AI-generated text, and also, it’s often unintentionally hilarious.) I’ve got a theory about why this happens, and I ran an experiment that generated some evidence to support it. But first… what, exactly, is Yoda-speak? Backwards, this bad writing is I’ve been working on my latest book. It’s called Be the Model , and it teaches you how LLMs work by having you build interactive pages that let you literally do the job of a model to get an intuitive understanding of how they work. So I’ve been writing a lot, which means I’ve been confronted with a lot of Yoda-speak. Here’s a great example from the chapter I’m currently working on (the “pond sentences” are a small training text), from a description of a page that you’ll build to learn how training works: The eight pond sentences fill the left region, every word clickable. That’s weird, right? Nobody talks like that. To be perfectly fair, I’ll need you to suspend your disbelief a little. Yoda would probably say something more like, “The left region, filled by the eight pond sentences is. Clickable, every word must be.” But the AI-generated version is still very weird, and in a pattern that is recognizably Yoda-like. That’s a pattern I’ve seen a lot. title: This implant can restore sight for patients with macular degeneration
abstract: More than 5 million people around the world with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) experience atrophy in their retinas. And until now, no treatment could restore their vision. The PRIMA system, which was approved in Europe in July and is awaiting FDA clearance in the US, changes that. It combines a retinal implant with camera-­equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision due to advanced AMD. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients were able to read, do crosswords, and use their phones. The retina processes light in three layers of cells: Photoreceptors convert light into electricity, bipolar cells process that signal, and ganglion cells transmit the signal to the optic nerve and the brain. PRIMA replaces the photoreceptors. BROWN BIRD DESIGN Developed by the California-based Science Corporation, the system takes advantage of the fact that AMD doesn’t damage all retinal circuitry; only photoreceptors—the cells that convert light into an electrical signal—die off. PRIMA’s implant mimics those cells and transmits visual information directly to healthy eye circuitry and on to the brain. “We’re leveraging all of the body’s own natural functions to process and transmit the information,” says Frank Brodie, an ophthalmologist at the University of California, San Francisco, and Science Corp.’s chief medical officer for ophthalmology. BROWN BIRD DESIGN CAPTURE Glasses outfitted with a miniature front-facing camera capture what someone is seeing in real time. The video feed is roughly five megapixels running at 30 frames per second, which is similar to TV. The raw video is transmitted to a connected processor via a fiber-optic cable . CONVERT A small, handheld processor, which can be set on a table or tucked in a pocket, converts the video feed into infrared light signals that route back to the glasses. The device also includes physical buttons that let the wearer adjust contrast, brightness, and zoom. BROWN BIRD DESIGN DISPLAY A laser projector on the glasses faces the wearer and shines pulses of near-infrared light directly at the eye at 880 nanometers—an invisible wavelength. This signal passes through the pupil and on to the retinal implant in the back of the eye. SEE The implant is made up of 378 pixels, each with an electrode and two photovoltaic cells , which do double duty. They convert the light into a current that healthy bipolar and ganglion cells pass on to the brain. They also act as solar cells to power the chip, eliminating the need for a battery. Update : This story has been updated to clarify the specific cases of AMD the PRIMA system treats. Linda Marsa is a former Los Angeles Times reporter and an author who covers medicine, health, science, and the environment.

title: Love is infrastructure
abstract: I. Meet cute Barnabas and Mainspring grew up near at hand, about an hour apart with good traffic, but for a long time they weren’t close. They traded glimpses and occasional hellos and then went about their business. Both of them carried on livelier conversations with farther-flung neighbors, who were richer and had more to offer. When Mainspring did interact with Barnabas, it was cringe. Mainspring liked to puff themself up, to strut around like a big deal—an innovator, a titan of industry—but they would turn shy at the worst moments, especially in any intimate conversation. Barnabas, meanwhile, had a dancer’s flair, an artsy, enigmatic glamour, except that when they tried to talk about real life, they’d blurt out hundreds of rapid-fire words—overtalking, overthinking, and generally overwhelming whomever they were trying to impress. So when Barnabas and Mainspring were young, they minded their own business. Until they’d both come into their own, and they saw each other properly. A group of geographers got together every year in a different place to talk about everything they had learned, and they were considering coming to visit either Mainspring or Barnabas. Both of them put on their best faces and tried to coax the geographers into choosing them as host. “Uh, hi-hello,” Mainspring said haltingly to Barnabas, whose full official name was St. Barnabas. “I really think it would be better if those geographers came to my place. I have more space, you see, and … and I am a titan of industry. I can show them practical applications of their research. It just makes more sense.” “Oh, really?” Barnabas laughed, making Mainspring more antsy. “Well, I can give them an elevated, artisanal experience. I have fresh croissants that were just written up in the Times . And I have plenty of space! I have so many friends who are great thinkers and architects. It’ll be lovely.” Barnabas carried on, basically calling Mainspring uncultured. Mainspring had a prickly feeling, like the worst heat dome of midsummer. For their part, Barnabas couldn’t bear the meanness they were inculcating inside themself. This feeling that they were small-time, no-account, a dilettante. They couldn’t stop aiming a flood of nervous words at Mainspring. At last, Mainspring had had enough—with the help of their city council and mayor, they offered the geographers a much-too-lavish deal that Barnabas could never hope to match. Totally worth it to hear Barnabas’s stream of self-aggrandizing nonsense peter out as they realized they’d been defeated. “There,” Mainspring said. “I’m going to show these geographers a time they’ll never forget. Now if you’ll excuse me, I’ve wasted enough energy—I have some sewer maintenance and a lovely parade to deal with. Goodbye.” Mainspring was skilled enough at multitasking that they could have fixed the sewer, ensured the smooth running of the parade, dealt with the geographers, and done a thousand other things all at the same time. But they were making a point. “St. Barnabas is such a fool,” Mainspring complained to their friend Turnbull. “They are totally unserious but determined to be taken seriously. It drives me to gridlock.” “I know what you mean,” lamented Turnbull. “We live in a world of posers.” Turnbull lived an hour and 15 minutes from Mainspring but at least two hours’ travel from Barnabas. Turnbull was even richer than Mainspring and had a certain surety of purpose that made Mainspring feel even more like a stammering numpty. “Whatever,” said Mainspring. “It’s over, and now I’ll never worry about St. Barnabas again. I have better things to fuss about. Like ensuring that every last detail of this geographer meeting goes perfectly.” II. How they came alive Everybody voted all the time. title: Can’t bear to say goodbye to your pet? Biotech’s got you covered.
abstract: I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat. I can conjure the sensation of stroking her while she purred, recall how she used to get stuck in trees (just like in cartoons!), and chuckle about the time she pooed in my baby sister’s cot. That’s about it. What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing. I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset. I made posters. We never found her. I was devastated. There was no way to get more time with Peppy, but almost 30 years later, pet owners are being offered an ever-expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions. The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics. But is that a good thing? There’s certainly a market for pet preservation. And a growing number of biotech companies have their sights set on pet longevity. Loyal, a company that is currently working on three potential longevity drugs for dogs, is trialing one designed to improve metabolic health in around 1,300 pet dogs across the US. Others are testing dog drugs that aim to combat both age-related diseases, including conditions like obesity and osteoarthritis , and aging itself. There’s even a company focused on longevity medicines for domesticated cats. I don’t know how or when Peppy died. But if there had been a drug that might have protected her from diabetes or arthritis, there’s no doubt I would have tried to get my hands on it. That’s about where my enthusiasm for pet life extension ends, though. I’m far less interested in cloning, a relatively new option for people mourning a pet and seeking a replacement. In most cases, this technology involves taking the DNA of a pet, putting it into an egg cell from another animal of the same species, and growing the resulting embryo in a surrogate animal. It worked for Dolly the sheep, who was born the year before Peppy went missing. It has since worked for other mammals, including cattle, horses, and ferrets—and cats and dogs. In the US, a company called Viagen Pets offers to clone cats and dogs for $50,000 a go. This doesn’t result in an exact replica of the animal but a genetic twin. Still, there are lots of reasons why a person might want to clone a pet. On its website, Viagen explicitly offers customers “a way to hold on.” Lori Kogan, a professor of clinical sciences at Colorado State University who has studied human-animal relationships for decades, doesn’t have a problem with the practice. She points out that while we have well-established rituals for coping with the loss of a person—such as funeral services, time off work, and memorial gifts—we don’t really have the same for pets. As a result, pet owners can experience what is sometimes called “disenfranchised grief,” she says. Having their feelings go unrecognized can feel isolating. If cloning a pet brings a person peace, she says, “who are we to judge?” Fair enough. But I can’t help thinking that pet loss in childhood might be different. It’s often the first time a child confronts death. Losing Peppy was a formative experience, and distressing though it was, I like to think it helped prepare me for losses I experienced in adulthood. I wouldn’t want my own children to think that death is not final, and that individuals can be replicated or replaced. Or, for that matter, revived, which is the promise behind pet cryonics. For a fee, a handful of companies offer to cool dead pets to extremely low temperatures and store them for long periods of time—even indefinitely. The idea is that at some point in the future, we’ll have invented incredible technologies that will not only bring your pet back to life but also cure whatever it died of. Alcor , a cryonics facility in Arizona, is currently storing the remains of hundreds of pets as well as people. It even recently announced it had cooled a small marsupial—its first pet sugar glider. title: Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve.
abstract: Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds. The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15. But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented. A study published earlier this year found that four in five teens under 16 made their way onto barred platforms. Teens have successfully explored many tactics for bypassing bans, from using a sibling’s face for ID to drawing fake facial hair. Some proponents of bans have called for an increased focus on enforcement that blocks these workarounds. But circumvention is a signal, not a nuisance or something to be simply deterred. The fact that kids are actively looking for ways to outwit the bans highlights their limitations. Social media bans suppress kids’ access to information, including information that’s essential to their development, identity formation, and socialization, especially during adolescence. Worse, further restriction is likely to backfire. Closing loopholes in age gates could harm kids by pushing them toward less-moderated, higher-risk corners of the web. It also degrades privacy and security for everyone by forcing people to submit sensitive personal information to prove their age. In our work , we’ve found that parents and kids both want smarter, more nuanced policies that protect children, families, and their rights. That can take the form of mandating stronger limits on data collection by companies, or giving families flexible tools to control content and access on their own terms. Age gates won’t bring about the desired change, nor will they simplify parenting in the digital world. At best, they will only raise thornier questions and postpone the conversation to a child’s 16th birthday. At worst, they’ll leave kids with no guidance as they make their way through the online world. A less safe internet for kids When young people circumvent restrictions, they are often doing what we want developing minds to do and what we celebrate in other contexts: lean into curiosity, problem-solve, and exercise independence. It’s important for kids to do this online, an arena where they often develop social skills and refine their identities . Bans sweep these motivations under the rug, taking a paternalistic approach that doesn’t consider young people’s needs or the realities of what they do online. It also ignores what some parents want. When we examined social media safety interventions last year, parents told us that they often join their kids in lies that help them gain access to needed but gated services. This isn’t a new phenomenon; research all the way back in 2011 showed that parents taught their children how to evade Facebook age restrictions. Some may say these parents are oblivious to the harms posed by the web or just don’t care. But parents are not a monolithic group. Many simply see offering their children responsible access to social media as a way to help them connect with like-minded peers, find informational content, and learn digital safety skills early on. Many parents believe the benefits outweigh the risks. When parents don’t help provide access and kids are not able to get into the platforms they desire, they will likely move toward alternative online spaces, often ones with fewer guardrails. Sometimes kids wind up on fairly innocuous, if unconventional , platforms, communicating with each other in Google Docs or podcast comment sections . Other times they move to more dangerous platforms that can leave them vulnerable to abuse and predation. Pig kidneys that were “frozen” for a year have been brought back to life Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150 °C and stored in a freezer for months have been successfully rewarmed and shown to work again for the first time, say scientists. The kidneys, which are similar in size to human ones, were left in a glass-like state, in one case for over a year. Once they had been rewarmed, tested in machines, and transplanted into pigs, the kidneys regained their color and made urine—key signs they were working. The results are a big milestone. But the team still needs to establish whether the approach could work for humans. title: How much more can nuclear power plants give?
abstract: In this age of rising electricity demand, people are trying to squeeze every last bit of power out of every power plant possible. Over the past few weeks, there’s been big news about nuclear power plants trying to do just that. Constellation, the largest nuclear operator in the US, announced plans to add nearly a gigawatt of new capacity across 11 existing nuclear reactors at six plants. And on October 5, the Department of Energy awarded a $4.2 billion loan to Vistra for previously announced upgrades at three plants. Pushing existing reactors to produce more could help provide more clean power for data centers, quickly. But just how much additional power can we count on? Upgrading equipment at existing nuclear power plants can allow them to reach a higher capacity; the process is called a power uprate. Operators have been doing this since the 1970s in the US, but it’s been less common in recent years as demand for electricity plateaued and cheap natural gas put financial pressure on nuclear power plants. Some plants closed, and putting in more money to produce more electricity didn’t make much sense at others. Between 2001 and 2010, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission approved over 80 uprates. Between 2011 and 2020, the number was 33. But with the rise of AI and the related boom in electricity demand, there’s been a shift. We’re seeing shuttered plants like Palisades and Three Mile Island race to reopen. And existing plants are looking to uprate again. Some uprates are minor, involving changes to instrument setpoints or calculations at the plant. But more major overhauls, which can boost reactor power by as much as 20%, require replacing plant equipment. Generally, uprates involve using fuel that’s more highly enriched, or a higher volume of fresh fuel, in the nuclear reactor. That helps produce more steam, which is used to turn a turbine and generate electricity. To handle that additional energy, the main turbines and equipment such as pumps, motors, generators, and transformers are upgraded. The most recent major uprate approved in the US was for three reactors at the Browns Ferry nuclear power plant in Alabama. A $475 million project saw that plant expand its power capacity by 14% between 2018 and 2019. Things could pick up soon, though. Constellation announced plans this week to spend more than $4.3 billion on uprates to 11 reactors. The additional electricity will be enough to power roughly 700,000 US homes. Behind it all? Big Tech money. Google agreed to buy electricity from these plants, and the 20-year agreement was a major factor in making the uprates happen. As Joe Dominguez, Constellation’s CEO, told the New York Times : “These are capital intensive, labor intensive projects that require a different price point than the market trades at, frankly.” Also in the last few weeks, the US Department of Energy shared that it will commit over $4 billion to help finance upgrades and modernization for Vistra nuclear power plants across Pennsylvania and Ohio. Those projects will add 433 megawatts of power capacity, and Meta has already signed on to buy electricity from the plants in a long-term deal. A note about cost: On a per-kilowatt basis, that Constellation project is less expensive than building a new reactor, but it’s still more expensive than building a new utility-scale solar farm with energy storage or a combined-cycle natural-gas plant. Even at this high cost, uprates are in high demand. Today, the US nuclear fleet has roughly 98 gigawatts of total power capacity. Depending on who you ask, there’s somewhere between three and eight additional gigawatts on the table from uprates. A pretty significant chunk of the potential uprates in the US are already accounted for—the NRC already expects applications to add 2.4 gigawatts of power to reactors through 2032. title: Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind
abstract: Have you ever thought about what makes you you ? Science assures us it has everything to do with the three-pound organ between our ears, with its billions of neurons and trillions of delicate connections. But it’s a lot trickier to explain why we have a sense of self-awareness or to pin down precisely where that first memory of Mommy actually resides. As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you. To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are working on ways to keep your brain going—even beyond death. Let’s call them the “mind savers.” They’re exploring everything from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones to uploading our memories to the cloud. Here, we look at six possible paths for keeping your mind going, how feasible they’d be, and what benefits the ­present-day research might bring—even if cognitive immortality doesn’t pan out. EDDIE GUY Head transplant White’s experiments have been a source of grim fascination ever since. But to a few neuroscientists they’re inspiration, suggesting that one day a human head transplant—or, as some call it, a body transplant—could succeed. The idea’s main proponent is Sergio Canavero, a controversial Italian surgeon who, 10 years ago, even claimed he’d found a volunteer in Valery Spiridinov, a computer programmer suffering from a degenerative muscle disease. Spiridinov initially agreed to have his head transferred to the body of a brain-dead donor in China, but he later bowed out of the plan and instead got married. And that might be just as well. Critics say the procedure would be more like murder than medicine. Or, best-case scenario: Volunteers would be left paralyzed and in need of a ventilator for life. Canavero says that’s not necessarily true. He claims people’s views on the operation will change once they accept that reconnecting severed spinal cords is already possible. He pointed MIT Technology Review to a research article from this past summer that he coauthored with surgeons at Moscow’s Sklifosovsky Research and Clinical Institute for Emergency Medicine. The team cut through the spinal cords of three pigs at a point midway along their backs and then tested whether the severed nerve bodies could be fused back together using a surgical sealant. According to that paper, which appeared in the journal PLOS One , all the pigs regained the ability to stand and even walk unsteadily. Does that mean a head could be attached to a new body and then actually control it? Mainstream researchers aren’t convinced. Grégoire Courtine, a spinal rehabilitation specialist at the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne in Switzerland, says he’s been following Canavero’s claims “with little respect” and thinks that we should “pay zero attention.” “There is no technology … capable of such a crazy idea,” Courtine wrote in an email. Mindclones Just 12 years after the book came out, artificial-intelligence technology has already brought some of her predictions to “life,” so to speak. Services such as StoryFile, Afterlife AI, and Synthesia allow users to upload their personal information and likeness in order to produce either conversational bots that share their memories or video talking heads that sound (and look) exactly like them. Influencers now let their “AI clones” do their work on TikTok, and some people are even building avatars of their aging parents in order to preserve their personalities. While this mimicry can produce comical results, unhealthy attachments, or uncanny vibes, the increasing realism of generative AI invites people to emotionally accept the avatars as real beings. That was the case when Rothblatt appeared as a digital avatar during a 2025 event held by the UCLA Department of Communication called “The Bridge to Humanizing AI.” Her copy, named Marvatar, was projected on a screen, led the discussions, and talked with the meatspace Ro

title: Pig kidneys that were “frozen” for a year have been brought back to life
abstract: Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150 °C and stored in a freezer for months have been successfully rewarmed and shown to work again for the first time, say scientists. They hope to replicate the findings with human organs. The kidneys—which are similar in size to human ones—were left in a glass-like state, in one case for over a year. Once they had been rewarmed, tested in machines, and transplanted into pigs, the kidneys regained their color and made urine—key signs they were working. “Ten years ago … I wouldn’t say I had high hopes it was actually going to work,” says Erik Finger, a transplant surgeon at the University of Minnesota who co-led the work. “After we did the last transplant, I walked out of the room and said, ‘This is a big deal.’” The research was shared at the preprint server bioRxiv and has not yet been peer-reviewed. The kidneys aren’t perfect, and the researchers have yet to demonstrate that they can sustain life over the long term. But the results represent a milestone achievement, say others in the field. “Thank God that someone’s actually managed to do it in one organ and prove that it works,” says Peter Kilbride, a cryobiologist and cofounder of Kyros Kairos, a company focused on improving funding for cryopreservation research, who was not involved in the research. “For years, people have been trying and failing to get to this step. Finally, we’ve got this breakthrough.” “Their work is amazing and will enable us to truly, indefinitely bank organs,” says Korkut Uygun, a biomedical engineer and professor of surgery at Harvard Medical School, who was also not involved in the research. “It is a revolutionary time for transplantation.” Buying time Every year, tens of thousands of organ transplants take place in the US alone. These procedures are thought to have saved 2 million years of life in the last 25 years . But there’s plenty of room for improvement. One major challenge is the lack of available organs. Even when an organ becomes available, it can be difficult to get it to the right recipient within 24 to 36 hours, which is the current limit for preserving human organs. People who receive organ transplants must also take drugs that suppress their immune systems for the rest of their lives. These drugs are meant to stop their bodies from rejecting the new organs. But they come with side effects and increase the risk of infections and cancer. The ability to bank organs for long periods of time holds the promise to address all these challenges. Doctors would have more time to match organs to recipients. They’d be able to limit the risk of organ rejection, too—potentially by preparing recipients, and their immune systems, beforehand. “With real organ banking … instead of the patients waiting for the organ, it’s the organs that are waiting for the patients,” says Finger. Scientists have been able to cool cells to ultra-low temperatures through a process called vitrification, which essentially turns them to something like glass. This procedure is already used to store eggs, sperm, and embryos. Vitrifying whole organs is much harder. Some problems can be avoided with cryoprotectants—chemicals that work like antifreeze and prevent damaging ice crystals from forming. But these chemicals tend to be incredibly toxic. It’s also difficult to rapidly and uniformly cool large tissues, and just as hard to evenly rewarm an organ all the way through. Working with John Bischof, a bioengineer at the University of Minnesota, Finger and colleagues have come up with a solution. Once an organ has been loaded with a cryoprotectant, they infuse it with iron oxide nanoparticles. These nanoparticles don’t do anything to the cells. But when it’s time to rewarm the organ, they can be activated with an electromagnetic field. When the radiofrequency of that field switches between two states, the particles also flip, realigning themselves with the field. That causes them to release heat throughout the organ. title: Simulation App Speeds Up Electric Truck Battery Design
abstract: This article is brought to you by COMSOL . These days, no one blinks an eye at two-day, one-day, and even same-day package deliveries. Despite the plethora of localized fulfillment and distributi on centers that have cropped up to meet the demand, delivery trucks still need to make considerably long drives, often over highways. To reduce fuel and maintenance costs as well as carbon emissions, companies are investing in electric trucks for their delivery fleets. While turning to electric trucks is a promising solution, the battery packs incorporated into these automotive designs often fall short in the lifetime needed to make long-distance highway travel feasible. To help overcome the issue of battery lifetime, a consortium of universities and industry partners incorporated multiscale simulation and a custom simulation app into the battery manufacturing process. The organizations involved in this project were Aurobay, Resolvent, the European Commission, the Technical University of Denmark (DTU), Vinnova (the Swedish Agency for Innovation Systems), Innovation Fund Denmark, and Volvo Group Trucks Operations. The simulation app, built by Resolvent, a Denmark-based engineering consultancy that specializes in green energy, enables the R&D department at Volvo to easily test battery lifetime performance. Laser Who? The Multiscale Simulation of Laser Welding for Optimal Battery Pack Manufacturing project — referred to as “LaserBATMAN” — was initiated in May 2022 and wrapped up in May 2025 (Ref. 1). Although BATMAN here refers to battery manufacturing and not the famous masked superhero, the goals for the project also strove for greatness. The LaserBATMAN project aimed to optimize two key performance metrics for battery packs: robustness and lifetime (Ref. 1). One element of the battery manufacturing process that affects both of these metrics is the laser welding used in component joining processes (for example, to connect battery cells in a pack via a busbar). If done correctly, laser welding can positively impact battery life, but if done incorrectly, laser welding can increase the risk of battery degradation. Computational modeling can be used to analyze and predict the effects of welding and joining processes at different stages of the manufacturing process. Martin Refslund Nielsen, former chief commercial officer and partner at Resolvent, explained that for this type of multiphysics and multiscale problem, “COMSOL Multiphysics is just the right tool.” R&D Workflow for Multiscale Model and App The Resolvent team used the COMSOL Multiphysics software to study how laser welding affects the electrochemistry and degradation of battery cells. At least, that’s how the project started. “Ambitions grew,” Nielsen said, explaining that the team ended up modeling the performance of the entire battery, from cell to pack level, and even “turned [the model] into a design tool in the end”, in reference to the app. After training the deep neural network of the battery model, the team built a custom simulation app to efficiently optimize busbar tabs in the configuration of a battery pack. First, the team built an electrochemical model of a battery cell by inputting the formulas for the relevant chemical reaction kinetics (Figure 2). The resulting cell-layer model was then fed input data, and the output data was used to train a deep neural network (DNN). With this reduced-order model, the team was able to quickly gain insight into cell behavior. After training the DNN of the battery model, the team built a custom simulation app to efficiently optimize busbar tabs in the configuration of a battery pack. Figure 2: The Resolvent battery model. COMSOL A “Tool Within a Tool” for Busbar Weld Design The different features of the simulation app, as described by Nielsen, include its options to input dimensions for the pack geometry (Figure 3), the number of cells, and operating conditions such as ambient temperature and charge–discharge current profiles. title: Bug turns one of the biggest fears about Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses into reality
abstract: Some Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses were recording people’s conversations without the wearer knowing. The recordings occurred without users saying the prompt phrase (“Hey, Meta”), in a bug that Meta says has been fixed. This week, some users reported online that their Ray-Ban Metas were recording without their consent. A person going by Kindly-Audience-137 on Reddit, for example, said this happened to them across three Meta Ray-Bans and that they had the “Respond without Hey Meta” setting turned off. The person said the Meta AI app “saves audio recordings and text transcripts of these conversations in my conversation history.” “I believe this deserves a serious technical investigation. Customers should not have to wonder whether their private conversations are being captured when they have not intentionally activated their glasses’ AI assistant,” the Reddit user said. title: RFK Jr. proposes FDA look the other way on unproven peptides, report says
abstract: Under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the Food and Drug Administration is moving forward with plans to ease access to unproven peptide drugs that are popular among members of Kennedy's Make America Healthy Again movement—despite FDA staff scientists finding that the drugs have not been sufficiently studied to establish safety and efficacy and may cause harms. The FDA submitted an "Interim Access Policy" on peptides for review by the White House, according to a filing notice posted on an Office of Management and Budget website. The posting does not provide information on the proposed policy. But people familiar with the proposal told The Associated Press that it would give the FDA "enforcement discretion" on certain peptide drugs. This would allow the agency to choose not to enforce current restrictions on peptides and provide an assurance to specialty pharmacies eager to start making them that they will not be targeted by the agency. The Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the FDA, did not respond to a request for comment from Ars Technica. Read full article Comments

title: Meta may use sweeping new commercial TOS to avoid millions in AI licensing fees
abstract: Legal experts are sounding alarms that Meta will soon update its commercial terms to require business accounts to allow Meta to train AI on their linked website content, not just their social media posts. Kicking in on October 30, the TOS update won’t allow businesses to opt out, instead suggesting that businesses stop using Meta services if they won’t agree to let Meta bots freely crawl their linked content. As Nieman Lab reported Thursday, this will affect all business accounts but is particularly shocking for news publishers who could perhaps charge Meta millions in licensing fees to continually access their articles for AI training. Currently news organizations are fighting a battle with OpenAI over whether such training without licensing is fair use, and Meta's terms seemingly risk granting it sweeping permissions, no matter which way the court leans. title: Polymarket saw $600 million in election trades after the elections were over
abstract: Prediction market boosters often tout the platforms as barometers of public opinion, or even “truth machines” offering a clearer picture of where things are headed than polling or other data. In 2024, for example, Kalshi beat many pollsters in forecasting the outcome of the US presidential race. But their trading activity can also tell more perplexing stories. Two global election markets on Polymarket’s offshore platform , for instance, generated over $600 million in trading volume, far more than most political markets typically attract. Most of the activity took place buying and selling contracts tied to long-shot candidates who ultimately did not win. This summer, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s Prosperity Party cruised to victory in federal elections, winning 438 parliamentary seats and paving the way for him to serve another five-year term. The closest competitor won 13 seats. On prediction markets, trading volume—the total value of contracts bought and sold—typically tracks roughly with the odds of a given outcome; frontrunners attract far more volume than long shots. But in this case, the trading patterns deviated sharply from the norm. Just $173,000 was wagered on Ahmed winning, compared to more than $41 million traded on his chief of staff, Shimelis Abdisa, becoming the country’s next leader. Altogether, the volume traded added up to over $285 million, nearly all on losing candidates. Read full article Comments

title: Tesla turns to 50-year-old stunt technology as it tries to Roadster again
abstract: Nine years after first trying to resurrect the Roadster , Tesla is apparently trying again. CEO Elon Musk might have relocated its HQ to Texas, but yet again he has returned to California’s showbiz industry to hawk his wares; last time it was a Hollywood back lot for the remote-controlled Cybercab demo , last night it was decades-old stunt technology to make a show car do tricks in the air. The new Roadster, we’re told, will be unlike anything else, although the angular, wedge-shaped styling owes more than a little to Giorgetto Giugiaro’s original Lotus Esprit—Musk is known to own a James Bond prop car—as well as the more recent Lamborghini Gallardo. At the rear are four giant exhaust pipes; these do not signal Tesla’s sudden embrace of hydrocarbons beyond those emitted by private aviation. Rather, it’s where 100,000 psi jets of compressed nitrogen shoot out. It’s early in the morning and the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Statutes are dense reading, so I am yet to find the section where it explains how and when it’s legal to use such a thing on the road. title: Super Scam Me documentary shows what it takes to catch a romance scammer
abstract: If you got a DM from an unverified Jon Bon Jovi account after commenting on one of his official Instagram posts, what would it take to make you believe it was really the rock star hoping to connect? And at what point when he starts asking you to send money—like lose-your-house kind of money—would you snap out of the fantasy and stop draining your bank account? In a documentary premiering Saturday— Super Scam Me —investigative journalist Mariana van Zeller goes deep into this toxic love-bombing terrain. In a clip that Ars is exclusively debuting below, you can see how van Zeller worked with an ethical hacker, Arman the Cyber, to use a fake bitcoin receipt and bait the fake Bon Jovi, giving the victim some much-needed closure. Sneak peek at National Geographic's Super Scam Me . Scamming a romance scammer Broadcasting on National Geographic at 9 pm ET and available to stream on Disney+ and Hulu, the documentary takes viewers on an empathetic quest to understand how the line between “lover” and “fraud victim” gets blurred in romance scams that the Federal Trade Commission says cost Americans nearly $1.5 billion in losses each year. title: The Surface Laptop Ultra delivers on most of Microsoft's promises
abstract: Over the past week, the laptop Microsoft sent me has been summarizing books and movies, generating images from my imagination, and running a 70-billion-parameter AI model that would be a stretch to fit on most laptops. It also played AAA games at a speed and fidelity I would have thought impossible on an ARM system just a year ago. Microsoft wants to sell you one computer for all of your needs, and for once that doesn't feel like total marketing fluff. Mostly. Microsoft is throwing both arms around the new Nvidia RTX Spark platform with the Surface Laptop Ultra—and setting its sights on the would-be MacBook Pro buyer, or as the company called it, "a high performance audience." The bet is that rather than a gaming desktop for fun and a development laptop for work, buyers will pay more for one machine that does both. The Surface Laptop Ultra arrives at a strange time in personal computing. Recent industry numbers showed a 20 percent drop in total PC shipments year over year in the third quarter of 2026. That's not just consumer purchasing either—that's across the board. Between the RAMpocalypse that has exploded consumer prices and an industry fixated on enterprise money, there hasn't been much new hardware to excite PC enthusiasts. Read full article Comments

title: Rocket Report: FAA eyes more Starbase traffic; India's Skyroot snares US customer
abstract: Welcome to Edition 9.15 of the Rocket Report! The launch I'm most looking forward to in the next few weeks is that of Japan's Martian Moons Exploration (MMX) mission. MMX is one of the marquee space science missions launching this year, and it's set to leave Earth as soon as Monday (US time) aboard a Japanese H3 rocket. The spacecraft will visit Phobos and Deimos, the two asteroid-like moons of Mars, deploying a rover and collecting specimens for return to Earth in 2031. Exploration at its finest. As always, we welcome reader submissions , and if you don't want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar. Reflect Orbital looks to India for launch capacity . California-based Reflect Orbital, the startup attempting to offer sunlight on-demand with in-space mirrors, announced the purchase of two launches Wednesday from Indian launcher Skyroot Aerospace, Payload Space reports . One of the launches will use Skyroot's Vikram-1 rocket, which became the first privately developed Indian rocket to reach orbit in July. The other will fly on an upgraded rocket called the Vikram-1U. title: Googlebook review: Android on a laptop is still Android
abstract: Android was designed for phones, but that hasn't stopped Google from trying to adapt the OS and its apps to larger machines over the years. Googlebooks are just the latest attempt after tablets, Chromebooks, and foldables induced little change in how people interact with Android software. These new Android-powered laptops are designed to pick up where the web-focused ChromeOS left off, offering premium hardware and native support for Android apps. Google sees Googlebooks as an alternative to Windows and macOS, but these platforms are entrenched with decades of software and UI conventions that keep users locked in. Googlebooks have to offer something very special to steal users away from either of the dominant operating systems. For devoted Android phone users, there are some cool things in Googlebook OS, but the Android roots of these machines are impossible to miss. Sometimes it feels like using a Chromebook, and sometimes it feels like using a giant phone. It almost never feels like using a premium laptop, and that's the problem. Read full article Comments

title: KDE turns 30 with Plasma 6.8, remote upgrades, and an X11 farewell
abstract: Marking the 30th anniversary of KDE on October 14, the project released Plasma 6.8, debuted a movie, and retired Plasma's native X11 session support. The announcement from KDE dubs the new Plasma 6.8 as the "30th Anniversary Edition" and describes the update as preparing Plasma for the future. Legacy X11 applications will still function via the XWayland compatibility layer , and KDE applications will also continue supporting X11 under other desktop environments. After 42 years in service, the X11 protocol is losing another major desktop environment. Plasma will fully adopt the Wayland system and put support for starting new X11 sessions in Plasma to bed. Users opting to stay on Plasma 6.7 will keep their existing sessions for now. The move was expected, with GNOME officially dropping X11 sessions by default in 2025 . The new Plasma 6.8 brings many improvements, including increased support for adding window decorations (like shadows and rounded corners) to third-party apps, and a more streamlined Union theming system . Other notable additions include Nvidia triple buffering being enabled by default, Kup backup integration (KDE's backup utility—now integrated into Plasma), and kscreenctl , a command-line utility that allows power users to adjust display configurations. title: Plex now helps sell movie theater tickets
abstract: Plex, which made a name for itself by letting users share movies they own, is now helping sell movie theater tickets. The company is looking to monetize its content-discovery capabilities and expand its business beyond its media server software. Plex partnered with Fandango, which has sold movie tickets since 2000, to drive ticket sales from people searching for movies to stream. Per the announcement: Starting today, Plex users in the US will see a Fandango ticketing option on title pages for movies currently playing in theaters, allowing them to click through to Fandango to find showtimes and purchase tickets. The integration also enables direct attribution through Kochava, giving studios and advertisers greater visibility into how campaigns and audience engagement translate into ticket sales. Fandango says it sells tickets for 31,000 movie theater screens in the US. The Plex deal allows it to leverage data from Plex’s streaming service (Plex claims users of the service “make more than 100 million streaming decisions each month”), including "ratings and cross-platform viewing" to gain “insight into audience intent," the announcement said. title: Hegseth’s dubious low-T screening may flag up to 25 percent of the Army
abstract: Up to a quarter of active-duty Army members could receive a low testosterone result from mandatory military screening, despite the true prevalence of the condition likely being a tiny fraction of that figure, according to a study published Thursday in JAMA . The finding adds to concerns that the mandatory screening announced by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in July will lead to a cascade of unnecessary medical evaluations for military members. Those evaluations could result in inappropriate testing, inaccurate results and diagnoses, and overtreatment that could cause harm, including infertility. Medical experts, including the Endocrine Society and the American Urological Association (AUA), have recommended against blanket screenings for these reasons. Still, the Pentagon has moved forward with the plans, releasing clinical guidance in September . The JAMA study highlights the reasons why testosterone levels are not measured in men without symptoms—and also offers a glimpse of how many Army members could become ensnared in the clinically dubious screenings. title: Targeted ads delivered 0-click exploits to install mercenary malware
abstract: Researchers say that mercenary hackers laced ads with zero-click exploits that installed sophisticated malware on the devices of targeted individuals when they did nothing other than load a website or open an installed app. The finding, published Thursday by the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, said the incident is likely to be the first confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through targeted ads. The attacks, which worked on iOS and Android devices, are particularly pernicious because they work without requiring any interaction from the target and are invisible unless users run special forensic hardware or software. Citizen Lab said it confirmed that AdFection, as it named the campaign, infected 45 devices at international media organization Al Jazeera in 2024 and 2025. A clear warning signal “This investigation should… serve as a clear warning signal to news organizations around the world that they may be being actively targeted via this new threat,” Citizen Lab researchers wrote. “This targeting may happen both in newsrooms and to individual journalists, editors, and other staff members.” Their report went on to say: “The distribution of spyware via targeted ads represents a security risk not only for potential victims but also for states and civil society at large.” Read full article Comments

title: Above the 911? Porsche previews a new mid-engined supercar.
abstract: Porsche showed us a preview of a new model this afternoon as it unveiled the Mission S concept in New York. It’s a mid-engined sports car that will slot into the Porsche range above the 911 . But this won’t be a limited-run car like the Carrera GT or 918 Spyder—instead it will be a regular production model, part of Porsche’s plan to dig itself out of a financial hole by 2035. Things have been tough for the German automaker of late. Just three years ago its profit margin was the envy of the industry at 18 percent; last year it collapsed to just 1 percent. It has recovered a little since then, and Porsche’s board has a plan to get back to double-digit margins by 2035, called “Sportwagenschmiede '35,” which involves prioritizing “value over volume,” with greater individualization for customers—and the associated higher selling prices that come with it. Note the quad exhausts—will this be powered by a flat-8? Credit: Porsche “We are pursuing a clear plan with our strategy Sportwagenschmiede '35. The ultimate goal is to further strengthen our unique sports car brand–across all model lines and with new, highly desirable models in particularly high-margin segments,” said Porsche Chairman Michael Leiters. title: What did the Liberty Bell sound like? Science is on the case.
abstract: The Liberty Bell , with its famous crack, hasn't been rung in 180 years, but that hasn't stopped scientists from pondering what the bell might have sounded like when tolling. In honor of the nation's 250th anniversary, researchers at Penn State University have modeled its acoustic properties, drawing on data collected from one of the bell's replicas. The work was first presented at a meeting of the Acoustical Society of America in Philadelphia earlier this year, followed by an article in Physics Today. Historians aren't sure exactly when the Liberty Bell acquired its distinctive crack, just that it occurred sometime between 1817 and 1846. An 1846 account in the Public Ledger described the ringing of the bell on February 23 that year and mentioned that the bell had developed a crack, which someone had attempted to fix by filing the sides down. But it didn't work: The February 23 ringing extended the crack even more, so much so that "the old Independence Bell ... now hangs in the great steeple irreparably cracked and forever dumb." Nobody has heard it ring since. This wasn't the first time the bell had cracked; the rim cracked shortly after it arrived in Philadelphia in 1752, the first time the clapper struck while testing the sound. It was recast by two local foundry workers, John Pass and John Stow, not once but twice, because the first recast produced a sound that one bystander likened to coal scuttles banging together. title: Black Sea drone attacks enter NATO country's territorial waters for first time
abstract: Russian drones are suspected of sinking a cargo ship and leaving chemical tankers ablaze near the Black Sea coasts of Bulgaria and Romania, respectively. The latest attacks mean that at least seven ships have been attacked in the exclusive economic zones of NATO member countries—and even within Romania's territorial waters if Russian involvement is confirmed in the case of the chemical tankers. Such attacks have spurred requests for NATO to redeploy counter-drone systems to provide more protection. In a social media post on October 15, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte stated that NATO had increased "counter-drone capabilities" along the alliance's eastern flank after meeting with the leaders of Bulgaria and Romania. The latest attacks this week occurred within 24 hours between October 14 and October 15, when the two chemical tankers were set afire after Russian drones were detected in Romanian airspace, according to Deutsche Welle . Both ships were sitting at anchor near the mouth of the Sulina canal that connects the Black Sea to the Danube River, which has become a crucial shipping export route for Ukraine, Reuters reported .
